title: Turn a falling weight into warming
question: Will the water warm if no hot object touches it?
explanation: The falling weight does work on the paddles. In this insulated model, every joule lost from its gravitational store becomes water internal energy.
limits: Ideal insulated calorimeter; the paddle timing is illustrative. Particle motion is magnified, not a molecular dynamics simulation.

title: A hot spoonful and a warm bucket
question: Which sample can transfer more energy while reaching room temperature?
explanation: Temperature changes the spread of particle speeds; it does not tell you how much water there is. Follow the amount bars when you change mass, then compare the energy bars for cooling to 30 °C. A tiny hot sample can release less energy than a warm bucket; enough hot water reverses that comparison. The equally enlarged marker windows show motion, not literal amounts.
limits: Both samples are liquid water with constant specific heat 4186 J/(kg K). Equal-size sampling windows and 64 markers per window are not physical volumes or molecule counts. The 3D amount bars and each diagram bar pair have a common linear scale; very small quantities make hairline bars. Maxwell curves describe classical translation, while water heat capacity includes interactions and other motion.

title: Insulation works in both directions
question: Will wrapping ice in a sweater melt it faster?
explanation: An insulating layer increases thermal resistance. It slows energy transfer from warm skin to a cool room, and from a warm room to cold ice.
limits: Steady one-dimensional conduction; convection and radiation are omitted. Layer thickness in the scene is enlarged.

title: Energy enters while the thermometer waits
question: During melting, where does the incoming energy go?
explanation: During a phase-change plateau, energy changes particle interactions and the phase fraction rather than increasing the temperature. Ice has an open structure; liquid water is denser near melting.
limits: One kilogram of pure water at atmospheric pressure. Ice and liquid arrangements are schematic; particle size stays fixed. Steam is represented as separate markers.

title: The fastest escape from a matka
question: Why does the same pot cool less below the air temperature in humid July?
explanation: Escaping water molecules remove energy. Humid air reduces net evaporation. The wet-bulb temperature is a lower limit for an ideal evaporative cooler under these conditions.
limits: Uses the book’s three illustrative weather cases, not live weather. Warm-water vaporisation cost is approximated as 2400 J per gram. The particle view illustrates selection, not measured rates.

title: A coastal circulation loop
question: What pushes warm air up above the land?
explanation: Warm air has fewer kilograms in the same volume at equal pressure. Cooler, denser surrounding air provides a buoyant upward push. The arrows show rising air over the warmer side, a return flow aloft and cooler air flowing in near the surface. Cool the land below the sea temperature to reverse the loop; equal temperatures remove this thermal drive.
limits: An illustrative sea-breeze loop, not a weather or monsoon forecast. Density uses the ideal-gas relation at a common pressure.

title: An engine needs a cold destination
question: Can all the energy from a hot reservoir become work in one cycle?
explanation: A cyclic heat engine transfers some incoming energy into work and rejects the rest to a colder reservoir. Even a reversible engine has the limit 1 − cold temperature / hot temperature, in kelvin.
limits: The animated piston illustrates a cyclic engine, not a pressure-volume calculation for a particular gas. Efficiency is a chosen fraction of the Carnot limit. The piston marks a repeated cycle schematically; its stroke is not a work measurement. The green output arrow vanishes at zero work; the paired energy bars supply the quantitative account.

title: What sets a pendulum’s clock?
question: Does increasing the mass shorten the period?
explanation: A heavier bob feels a larger gravitational pull, but it is harder to accelerate by the same factor. Dividing tangential force by mass gives the same acceleration at the same angle. Red arrows show gravitational g; green arrows show the acceleration along the arc. The string also keeps the bob on its circular path. The readout keeps actual forces in newtons. Length changes the clock; mass does not.
limits: Point bob and massless string; no damping. The amplitude correction is valid for the offered angles up to 40 degrees. The displayed swing is a harmonic motion at the corrected period, rather than an exact nonlinear integration. Red gravitational g and green tangential-acceleration arrows use one fixed scale for both bobs; they do not depict total acceleration or force. Their tails are offset outside the bob for visibility.

title: Push in time, then add damping
question: Can the same small drive produce different amplitudes?
explanation: A periodic force adds energy efficiently near the natural rhythm. In steady motion, input per cycle balances damping losses. Stronger damping limits the response.
limits: Linear oscillator with RK4 transient motion, drive work and damping loss. The separate amplitude curve is the steady response; a manual impulse acts on the current transient.

title: A steady flow can feed a twist
question: Does the wind need to arrive in rhythmic gusts?
explanation: A twisting deck changes how the steady wind pushes on it. If the wind’s turning push tends to act in the same direction as the deck’s motion, it adds energy on average. Damping removes energy. When input wins, the twist grows without the wind needing rhythmic gusts.
limits: A prescribed small-amplitude torsional energy model, not a CFD model or reconstruction of Tacoma’s collapse. It shows feedback separately from externally timed resonance. The plotted energy is a cycle-averaged envelope. The side inset enlarges the central twist angle fourfold and states the actual angle; the 3D deck uses the unscaled angle.

title: Follow a parcel beneath a wave
question: Does a marked parcel travel with the crest?
explanation: Watch the red parcel circle the black mean-position mark in the enlarged inset. A crest travels onward, but that parcel returns near its starting place. The inset is the same surface motion enlarged40× in both directions. The whole-wave view keeps the smaller physical displacement; deeper parcels move less.
limits: Linear deep-water gravity wave; controls keep kA≤0.189. The framed 3D local copy and the right-hand calculated inset magnify displacement40× in both directions, with the same clock and the same parcel state as the main view. No Stokes drift, breaking or finite-depth dispersion.

title: A compression crosses the air
question: Will one air particle travel from the speaker to your ear?
explanation: Watch the red air parcel: it moves back and forth near the black mean position while the pattern travels on. Blue shows pressure; red shows local displacement, each divided by its own maximum. Pressure is highest where neighbouring parcels crowd together, not where one parcel is furthest from its mean. Those two peaks are a quarter of a wavelength apart.
limits: A one-dimensional plane sound wave shown inside a volume. Regular marker rows represent mean positions, not a frozen molecular lattice; random thermal motion is omitted. Motion and time are magnified/slowed.

title: One clap, two legs of the journey
question: If the echo returns after 0.29 seconds, did sound travel one wall-distance or two?
explanation: The same pulse travels to the reflecting wall and returns. Distance to the wall is sound speed times return delay divided by two.
limits: Ideal flat reflector, sound speed 349 m/s for the warm-air example. The pulse drawing is not a pressure amplitude measurement.

title: Two separate sound controls
question: Can a higher-pitched sound also be quieter?
explanation: Frequency controls pitch; amplitude controls the oscillation size. At fixed medium, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.
limits: Synthetic sine tone, never a calibrated sound-level meter. Playback is optional and stops when this experiment closes or leaves view.

title: A drumhead has nodal lines
question: How does a circular skin differ from a string?
explanation: A node is a line or point that stays still while nearby parts of the skin move. The clamped rim must stay still too, so only certain vibration patterns fit. A circular skin does not give the evenly spaced frequencies of a string. Added central mass slows each pattern according to how much that part of the skin moves.
limits: Uniform membrane modes are calculated. The central-load case uses a Rayleigh trial-shape estimate, not an exact tabla simulation; it does not force the frequencies onto integer multiples. The same calculated frequency drives optional audio.

title: Choose who hears the moving horn
question: What does the driver hear compared with the platform listener?
explanation: Each wavefront expands from its emission position through the air. A listener moving with the source receives the emitted frequency; a stationary listener ahead receives crests more often.
limits: One-dimensional radial Doppler relation in still air; offered speeds remain subsonic. Drawn crests sparsely sample the actual sound wave. The still view begins after several crests have already been emitted. The repeating animation resets its time window.

title: Light must arrive at the eye
question: Will an eye looking harder reveal an unlit mango?
explanation: A source illuminates the object. Some scattered light enters the eye. Removing the source or blocking that route removes the signal; nothing is emitted by the eye.
limits: Ray samples show possible light directions, not visible threads in clean air. The model view keeps apparatus visible even when the signal is zero.

title: Open the camera and follow the rays
question: Will making the hole larger improve both brightness and sharpness?
explanation: Straight rays from each object point cross through the opening to the opposite screen position. A finite opening gives each point a blur disc; enlarging it admits more light and more geometric blur.
limits: Geometrical optics only; very-small-hole diffraction and exposure are omitted. Object and screen dimensions are shown numerically. The 3D apparatus is an opened camera cutaway; longitudinal framing and aperture enlargement in the lower diagram are named.

title: A large lamp softens a shadow
question: Is a fuzzy shadow edge always diffraction?
explanation: Different points on an extended source cast displaced shadows. Umbra receives none of the source; penumbra receives only part.
limits: Geometric projection from a sampled line source. Light diffraction and multiple scattering are omitted.

title: Walk around a mirror image
question: Is the image painted on the glass?
explanation: Reflected rays obey equal angles. Their backward extensions meet at a virtual image behind a flat mirror. Curved mirrors can form real or virtual images depending on object distance.
limits: Flat-mirror paths are geometrical. The spoon comparison is an ideal paraxial concave/convex mirror; a real spoon has aberrations.

title: Bring back the hidden coin
question: Can water make the coin visible while eye and coin stay fixed?
explanation: Refraction at the surface creates a route past the rim. Back-projecting the arriving ray gives a shallower apparent position, while the real coin stays on the bottom.
limits: Illustrative tumbler dimensions; Snell’s law solves the surface crossing. The empty/full comparison keeps eye, coin and rim fixed.

title: Guide light around a bend
question: At which surface angle will the ray start leaking out?
explanation: A ray can reflect internally when it meets a higher-to-lower-index boundary beyond the critical angle. The path changes direction at successive contacts, not continuously between them.
limits: Exact two-dimensional ray intersections with a circular annulus, visualised as a bent light guide. Absorption and diffraction are omitted.

title: Why goggles restore underwater vision
question: Why does water blur an eye that works in air?
explanation: The air–cornea index jump supplies much of the focusing. Water reduces this jump. Goggles restore an air layer and the cornea’s refracting power.
limits: Reduced thin-lens teaching eye, not a prescription. Rays, focus and retinal intercepts use one physical conjugate state. Incoming rays are clipped near the eye; transverse scale is enlarged independently. The retinal image uses the calculated angular scale and pupil blur diameter; the Gaussian blur rendering is illustrative. The retinal inset shows one point’s spread on a fixed 1 mm reference scale, with a small centre marker kept visible at zero blur.

title: Emission time is not arrival time
question: Can the same eclipse be observed at different times from different distances?
explanation: An event emits a signal at one time; arrival occurs after distance divided by light speed. Changing Earth’s position changes the light-travel delay.
limits: Circular coplanar Earth/Jupiter geometry with schematic Io eclipse events; not an ephemeris or reconstruction of Rømer’s fitted observations.

title: A cogwheel times a light round trip
question: How fast must the next tooth replace the outgoing gap?
explanation: Light leaves through a gap and makes the journey to the distant mirror and back. Meanwhile the wheel turns. At the first fully dark return, the neighbouring tooth has replaced that gap and blocks the returning light. The known tooth spacing, wheel speed and round-trip distance tell us how long the light took.
limits: Equal-width teeth and gaps; transmission averages launch and return openings over a wheel cycle. The marker follows one ray launched at the gap centre. Full extinction occurs at gap-to-tooth centre alignment. Predicts timing with modern c; Fizeau’s approximate observed speed was 12.6 Hz. Apparatus and tiny phase advance are separately magnified.

title: Select one colour for the second prism
question: Will a second prism add colours to selected red light?
explanation: The first prism separates wavelengths because its refractive index depends on wavelength. Selecting one narrow band leaves that band alone; the second prism refracts it without inventing other wavelengths.
limits: A 60-degree ideal crown-glass prism; index interpolated between red and violet textbook values. Ray directions follow the calculated refractions. Apparatus dimensions are schematic.

title: One drop becomes a rainbow cone
question: Where must the Sun be relative to the observer?
explanation: A primary-rainbow ray refracts into a drop, reflects once, and refracts out. Drops sending light towards one observer lie on a cone around the antisolar direction.
limits: Spherical water drops, one internal reflection and wavelength-dependent index. The scene shows a selected impact parameter, not a complete intensity calculation.

title: The spectrum an object returns
question: Will the banana remain yellow under blue-only light?
explanation: The returned spectrum is the illuminating spectrum multiplied by the object’s reflectance. Broad overlapping cone sensitivities combine the returned wavelengths into colour responses.
limits: Illustrative smooth spectra and cone sensitivity curves; screen RGB cannot reproduce every real spectrum or visual adaptation.

title: Direct light and scattered light take different routes
question: Is blue sky simply sunlight viewed straight through blue air?
explanation: Short wavelengths scatter more strongly. The sky receives light redirected into the eye; a long direct path removes more blue from the light that continues towards the observer.
limits: Uniform 8 km effective-air shell for optical depth; drawn shell enlarged. Scattering event lies inside air and both incoming rays share the Sun direction. Removed fraction includes all scattered directions, not a prediction of light entering one eye.

title: Turn the filter and delete the glare
question: Does rotating a filter change all light by the same amount?
explanation: A filter transmits the projection of the electric field onto its axis. Intensity follows the squared projection. Fresnel reflection makes water glare strongly polarised near Brewster’s angle.
limits: Ideal analyser; incoherent Fresnel s/p intensities add. Water incidence/reflection is geometric; fields enlarged 5×. Separate unpolarised returning-water colour is set to illustrative 0.080 incident units and always halves through the analyser.

title: Probe the path difference
question: What path difference makes a dark point on the screen?
explanation: When crests arrive together, the two waves reinforce. If one route is half a wavelength longer, its crest arrives with the other wave’s trough and equal amplitudes cancel. Adding whole wavelengths brings them back into step. Move the probe to connect that route difference with bright and dark points.
limits: Exact source-to-probe distances; point-like coherent slits with equal amplitudes. The single-slit envelope and coherence loss are separate effects. The route sketch enlarges transverse distances independently. Each blue/yellow arrival arrow has half the common normalised amplitude; their red resultant has squared length equal to the plotted intensity.

title: Change an opening, a grating or a thin film
question: Does every rainbow-coloured object use a prism?
explanation: Waves leaving different parts of an opening reach the same screen point by different routes. They reinforce or cancel according to those route differences. A grating repeats the openings; a thin film supplies two reflected routes, including a phase reversal at one boundary. Changing spacing or thickness therefore selects different bright directions or colours.
limits: Fraunhofer model: 64 equal midpoint samples across one slit, eight equal grating sources, or two equal reflected film amplitudes. Plots and visible phasors use identical sums. Film one-reflection phase reversal is included; longitudinal and transverse apparatus scales are framed separately.

title: A bright spot in the middle of a shadow
question: What happens when equal-length rim paths meet at the centre?
explanation: At the centre, contributions from all around a circular obstacle’s rim arrive in phase. A near-axis rim-wave calculation predicts a central maximum.
limits: Near-axis paraxial rim model, 96 coherent samples converging to J₀²; not full Fresnel irradiance. Disc and probe transverse scales are separately enlarged; both geometry and phase use the selected physical radius.

title: Account for a changed photon colour
question: If the outgoing photon loses energy, what gains it?
explanation: Compare the two bars on one energy scale. When the outgoing photon has less energy, the molecule gains exactly the difference as vibration: this is Stokes scattering. In anti-Stokes scattering the vibration supplies energy to the outgoing photon. Elastic scattering transfers no net vibrational energy. A longer outgoing wavelength means a smaller photon energy.
limits: Schematic vibrational energy levels and selectable Raman shift. Shifted peaks are magnified; no assertion of an actual molecule’s spectrum or classical photon path.
